title: The Nuremberg trial opens
pull: Day one: the charges, read aloud

facts.text: On 20 November 1945 the International Military Tribunal opened its trial of the major Nazi war criminals in the Palace of Justice in Nuremberg, Germany.
Nuremberg was picked partly because the Palace of Justice was still largely intact and had a prison attached, and partly as a symbol: it had been the city of the Nazi Party rallies.
Four powers sat in judgment: the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union, each with a judge and an alternate. The British judge, Lord Justice Geoffrey Lawrence, presided.
Lawrence opened by telling the court the trial was "unique in the history of the jurisprudence of the world and it is of supreme importance to millions of people all over the globe."

The whole first day went to reading the indictment aloud. Prosecutors from all four nations took turns: the Americans read Count One, Sir David Maxwell Fyfe of Britain read Count Two, and French and Soviet prosecutors read the war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Hermann Goering, Rudolf Hess, Joachim von Ribbentrop, and Wilhelm Keitel sat in the front row of the dock, with American military police in white helmets standing behind them.
Everything was interpreted at once into English, Russian, French, and German. IBM supplied the microphones and headsets free of charge, and listeners chose a language by switching channels.
The interpreters, 36 of them in three teams of 12, took turns. A yellow light told a speaker to slow down; a red one stopped the proceedings.
The next morning the defendants entered their pleas and the American chief prosecutor, Robert H. Jackson, opened the case. The trial ran until the verdicts of 1 October 1946.

photoNote: Looking down on the defendants' dock: front row Goering (turned toward camera), Hess, von Ribbentrop, and Keitel; back row Doenitz, Raeder, von Schirach, and Sauckel; white helmeted American MPs behind. National Archives 238-NT-612 (NAID 540128), RG 238, use Unrestricted, US government work, public domain (also on Commons as 'Nuremberg Trials. Defendants in their dock...'). Dated only 'circa 1945 to 1946' by NARA, so it is not proven to be the opening day; the credit says 'during the trial'. 1920 x 1487 grayscale from the 3000 px TIFF, border trimmed. Frame on Goering and the front row. A true opening day image exists but is weaker: Truman Library 2004-433 (NAID 350375630), the packed courtroom with a prosecutor reading the indictment, only about 240 KB and NARA marks its use 'Undetermined'.
photoCredit: The defendants' dock at the Nuremberg trial, with Goering, Hess, Ribbentrop, and Keitel in the front row, 1945 to 1946. National Archives 238-NT-612, public domain.

declassified.fact: One defendant missed the opening. Ernst Kaltenbrunner, the former head of the Reich Security Main Office, was taken to hospital on 18 November 1945 with bleeding inside his skull, so the tribunal announced he was ill and carried on without him. He was back in hospital again on 18 December.

film.license: Public domain, U.S. government work (U.S. Army). NARA flags the film 'Restricted, Possibly' because of the captured German film it quotes; the courtroom footage is U.S. Army Signal Corps.
film.date_note: Courtroom film from the opening days of the trial, November 1945; the caption should say film of the courtroom at Nuremberg, not of the morning of 20 November itself.
